subject: biology
topicDisplay: B1–B2 — Form and function: molecules and cells
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Why carbon can build so many different molecules
Condensation joins monomers into polymers
Hydrolysis splits polymers back into monomers
Starch and glycogen store energy compactly
Cellulose: straight chains bundled into a strong wall
Glycoproteins let cells recognize each other
Double bonds, melting point and where fats are stored
Adipose tissue: energy store and insulator
Steroids slip through the bilayer
Condensation makes dipeptides and longer chains
Heat and pH change a protein's shape
Phospholipids form a bilayer by themselves
Osmosis and aquaporins
The fluid mosaic model
What counts as an organelle, and how their jobs were found
Why compartments help the cytoplasm
From one fertilized egg to many cell types
Totipotent, pluripotent, multipotent
Human cells come in very different sizes
Surface area against volume limits cell size

questions.q: A student measures the diameter of a cell as 7 µm. What is this diameter in nanometres?
options: 70 nm, because each prefix is ten times the next
7000 nm, because one micrometre is 1000 nanometres
0.007 nm, because a smaller unit means a smaller number
7 000 000 nm, because a micrometre is 10⁻³ of a metre
optionWhy: A student who treats each SI prefix as a factor of ten picks this. Micro is 10⁻⁶ and nano is 10⁻⁹, so the two differ by a factor of 1000, not 10.
1 µm = 10⁻⁶ m and 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m, so 1 µm = 1000 nm. The length is unchanged; it is expressed in a smaller unit, so the number is larger: 7 × 1000 = 7000 nm.
A student who divides because "nano is smaller" picks this. A smaller unit fits into the same length more times, so converting micrometres to nanometres multiplies by 1000.
A student who has swapped milli and micro picks this, treating 7 µm as 7 × 10⁻³ m. Micro is 10⁻⁶, so 7 µm is 7 × 10⁻⁶ m, which is 7000 nm.
questions.explain: 1 µm = 10⁻⁶ m and 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m, so 1 µm = 1000 nm. The length is unchanged; it is expressed in a smaller unit, so the number is larger: 7 × 1000 = 7000 nm.

questions.q: Two monosaccharides are joined by a condensation reaction to form a disaccharide. What happens in this reaction?
options: A molecule of water is taken in and split to supply the atoms that join the monomers
A hydrogen bond forms between the two monomers, holding them together as a disaccharide
Water dissolves the two monomers so that they meet, but no water is formed or used
A covalent bond forms between the monomers and a molecule of water is released
optionWhy: A student who has the two reactions swapped picks this. Water is used and split in hydrolysis, which breaks bonds; condensation forms a bond and releases water.
A student who thinks of hydrogen bonds as the bond of biology picks this. The bond formed by condensation is a strong covalent bond, which is why the disaccharide is stable until it is hydrolysed.
A student who sees water only as the solvent picks this. Water is a product of condensation: one molecule is released for every bond formed.

In a condensation reaction an -OH from one monomer and an -H from the other are removed and combine to form water, leaving a covalent (glycosidic) bond between the monomers. Repeated condensations build a polysaccharide.
questions.explain: In a condensation reaction an -OH from one monomer and an -H from the other are removed and combine to form water, leaving a covalent (glycosidic) bond between the monomers. Repeated condensations build a polysaccharide.

questions.q: A polypeptide made of 100 amino acids is completely hydrolysed into free amino acids. How many water molecules are used in the process?
options: 99 water molecules
100 water molecules
1 water molecule
0 water molecules
optionWhy: A chain of 100 amino acids contains 99 peptide bonds. Each hydrolysis reaction breaks one bond and uses one water molecule, which is split to supply the -H and -OH added to the products, so 99 water molecules are used.
A student who counts one bond per monomer picks this. Bonds lie between monomers, so 100 monomers are joined by 99 bonds, and hydrolysing them uses 99 water molecules.
A student who reads "polymer + water → monomers" as a single reaction picks this. Each bond needs its own hydrolysis reaction and its own water molecule.
A student who thinks water is merely the solvent picks this. Water is a reactant in hydrolysis: one molecule is consumed and split for every bond broken.
questions.explain: A chain of 100 amino acids contains 99 peptide bonds. Each hydrolysis reaction breaks one bond and uses one water molecule, which is split to supply the -H and -OH added to the products, so 99 water molecules are used.

questions.q: In glycogen a branch occurs roughly every 10 glucose monomers; in the amylopectin of starch a branch occurs roughly every 25 monomers, and amylose is unbranched. Animals often need to release glucose from their stores very rapidly. Which explanation best accounts for the high degree of branching in glycogen?
options: Branches shield the glycosidic bonds, slowing hydrolysis so that the store is released steadily over time
Monomers are removed by hydrolysis at chain ends, so more branches give more ends to act on at once
Branching makes glycogen non-polar, so that it remains insoluble until the glucose is actually required
Each branch point adds a bond in which extra energy is stored for release when the bond is broken
optionWhy: A student who sees branches as protection picks this. Branches expose more chain ends, speeding hydrolysis; a store that was released slowly would not suit an animal needing glucose quickly.

Glucose is removed from a polysaccharide only at the ends of chains. Every branch point creates an extra end, so a molecule with a branch every 10 monomers can be hydrolysed at many more points simultaneously than amylopectin, matching an animal's need for rapid mobilization.

A student who explains insolubility by non-polarity picks this. Glycogen is a polar molecule covered in hydroxyl groups; it is relatively insoluble because of its size, and branching has nothing to do with polarity.

A student who believes bonds store energy picks this. Breaking glycosidic bonds absorbs a little energy rather than releasing it; the energy comes from oxidizing the glucose released, however many branches there are.
questions.explain: Glucose is removed from a polysaccharide only at the ends of chains. Every branch point creates an extra end, so a molecule with a branch every 10 monomers can be hydrolysed at many more points simultaneously than amylopectin, matching an animal's need for rapid mobilization.

questions.q: Amylose, a polymer of alpha-glucose, forms a coiled chain, whereas cellulose, a polymer of beta-glucose, forms a straight chain. Why does the cellulose chain not coil?
options: Beta-glucose has a different molecular formula, and its extra atoms make the chain rigid
Covalent bonds between neighbouring cellulose chains pull each chain out straight and flat
Each beta-glucose is rotated 180° relative to its neighbours, so the chain is straight
Branches along the cellulose chain, as in amylopectin, prevent the chain from coiling
optionWhy: A student who believes alpha- and beta-glucose are different sugars picks this. Both are C₆H₁₂O₆; they differ only in the orientation of one -OH group, and that alone produces the alternating, straight chain.

A student who expects covalent cross-links picks this. Neighbouring chains are linked only by hydrogen bonds, and the straightness of each chain comes from the alternating orientation of its own monomers.

In beta-glucose the -OH on carbon 1 points above the ring, so successive monomers must alternate in orientation (each rotated 180°) to form the glycosidic bond. The alternating orientation cancels any tendency to curve, giving straight chains that can be bundled and cross-linked by hydrogen bonds.
A student who transfers the structure of starch to cellulose picks this. Cellulose chains are unbranched; they are straight because of the alternating orientation of beta-glucose monomers.
questions.explain: In beta-glucose the -OH on carbon 1 points above the ring, so successive monomers must alternate in orientation (each rotated 180°) to form the glycosidic bond. The alternating orientation cancels any tendency to curve, giving straight chains that can be bundled and cross-linked by hydrogen bonds.

questions.q: The ABO blood groups depend on glycoproteins on the surface of red blood cells. Which statement about these ABO antigens is correct?
options: The A and B antigens differ only in the sugar at the end of their carbohydrate chain
The A and B antigens are two entirely different proteins with unrelated amino acid sequences
Group O red blood cells carry a third antigen, the O antigen, in the place of the A or B
The carbohydrate part of each antigen projects inwards into the cell's cytoplasm
optionWhy: ABO antigens are glycoproteins with a shared base carbohydrate chain. The alleles of the ABO gene encode enzymes that add different terminal monosaccharides to that chain, producing the A or the B antigen, and it is this small difference in the carbohydrate that other cells and antibodies recognize.

A student who thinks of antigens only as proteins picks this. The identity of an ABO antigen lies in its carbohydrate chain, not its protein; A and B share the same base and differ in one terminal sugar.
A student who extends the A/B naming pattern to O picks this. Group O cells carry the unmodified base chain and neither the A nor the B antigen; there is no O antigen.

A student who has not registered the orientation of glycoproteins picks this. The carbohydrate faces outwards from the cell surface, which is what allows it to act in cell–cell recognition and to be met by antibodies.
questions.explain: ABO antigens are glycoproteins with a shared base carbohydrate chain. The alleles of the ABO gene encode enzymes that add different terminal monosaccharides to that chain, producing the A or the B antigen, and it is this small difference in the carbohydrate that other cells and antibodies recognize.

questions.q: A student analysed two energy stores. Oil from a plant seed contained 12% saturated and 88% unsaturated fatty acids; fat from a mammal's adipose tissue contained 55% saturated and 45% unsaturated fatty acids. At 20°C the oil was liquid and the fat was solid. Which explanation best accounts for the difference?
options: The mammal's fat must be solid inside its body, so it requires the higher melting point that a high proportion of saturated fatty acids provides, whereas the seed's oil only needs to be liquid at room temperature

The mammal keeps a high, constant body temperature at which a store rich in saturated fatty acids stays fluid enough, while the seed is at lower environmental temperatures and needs unsaturated fatty acids with low melting points
The mammal's fat is solid because saturated fatty acids contain many C=C double bonds, which raise the melting point, whereas the unsaturated fatty acids of the oil have none and so remain liquid

The oil is liquid because its unsaturated fatty acids have fewer hydrogen atoms and so fewer covalent bonds to break when they melt, whereas the mammal's saturated fatty acids have more bonds to break and stay solid
optionWhy: A student who judges the state of a stored fat at room temperature picks this. The relevant temperature is the mammal's body temperature, at which its fat is sufficiently fluid; being solid at 20°C says nothing about its state at 37°C.

Saturated fatty acids raise the melting point; unsaturated ones lower it. An endotherm maintains a body temperature well above 20°C, so a store with a high proportion of saturated fatty acids remains sufficiently fluid inside it. A plant is at environmental temperature, which is often low, so its store must be an oil rich in unsaturated fatty acids that stays liquid.

A student who thinks "saturated" means full of double bonds picks this. Saturated fatty acids have no C=C bonds and pack closely, which is why they raise the melting point; it is the unsaturated fatty acids that have C=C bonds.

A student who thinks melting breaks covalent bonds picks this. Melting leaves every molecule intact and only overcomes the attractions between molecules; the oil melts lower because the kinks from its C=C bonds stop the chains packing closely.
questions.explain: Saturated fatty acids raise the melting point; unsaturated ones lower it. An endotherm maintains a body temperature well above 20°C, so a store with a high proportion of saturated fatty acids remains sufficiently fluid inside it. A plant is at environmental temperature, which is often low, so its store must be an oil rich in unsaturated fatty acids that stays liquid.

questions.q: A seal living in polar seas has a layer of adipose tissue (blubber) several centimetres thick beneath its skin. A dolphin of similar size living in tropical seas has a much thinner layer, and a cod living in the same polar seas as the seal has very little adipose tissue beneath its skin. Which explanation accounts for all three observations?
options: All animals in cold water need thick insulation, so the cod must have an equally thick layer of fat elsewhere in its body to keep itself warm in the polar sea
Blubber generates the heat that keeps the seal warm in polar water, the dolphin needs to generate less heat in warm water, and the cod does not generate any heat at all
Blubber traps a layer of air against the skin, the dolphin's warmer water means that less air is needed, and the cod's scales cannot hold a layer of air in place under water
Adipose tissue slows heat loss, so an endotherm needs more of it the larger the gap between its body and habitat temperatures, and the cod's body is at almost the temperature of the water
optionWhy: A student who links insulation to habitat alone picks this. The cod is an ectotherm with a body temperature close to the water's, so a fat layer could not keep it warm; only endotherms, whose bodies are warmer than their habitat, benefit from thick insulation.

A student who thinks fat produces warmth picks this. Blubber does not generate heat; it slows the loss of heat produced by metabolism. Its thickness reflects how much heat loss must be prevented, not how much heat must be made.

A student who transfers the trapped-air mechanism of fur and feathers picks this. Blubber contains no air; the triglyceride-filled tissue is itself a poor conductor, which is why it insulates under water where trapped air would be lost.

Blubber is a poor conductor of heat, so it reduces the rate of heat loss from a warm body to colder surroundings. The seal maintains a body temperature far above that of polar water and needs thick insulation; the dolphin in warm water loses heat more slowly and needs less; the cod is an ectotherm at almost the temperature of the water, so insulation would retain no heat.
questions.explain: Blubber is a poor conductor of heat, so it reduces the rate of heat loss from a warm body to colder surroundings. The seal maintains a body temperature far above that of polar water and needs thick insulation; the dolphin in warm water loses heat more slowly and needs less; the cod is an ectotherm at almost the temperature of the water, so insulation would retain no heat.

questions.q: Four molecules are drawn as molecular diagrams. Which description identifies the molecule that is a steroid?
options: A single six-membered ring made up of five carbon atoms and one oxygen atom
A chain of amino acids folded up into a compact globular shape
Four fused rings of carbon atoms, three with six atoms and one with five
A glycerol backbone joined to three long hydrocarbon chains
optionWhy: A student who treats any ring as the mark of a steroid picks this. A single ring containing an oxygen atom, with carbon outside it, is the ring form of a hexose such as glucose.
A student who thinks steroid hormones are proteins picks this. A folded amino acid chain is a protein; steroids are lipids with four fused rings and no amino acids.

A steroid is recognized by its four fused rings sharing edges, three six-membered and one five-membered. Oestradiol and testosterone both have this structure, which is non-polar and lets them pass through the phospholipid bilayer.
A student who equates lipids with fats picks this, choosing the fat. This is a triglyceride; steroids are a different class of lipid with a fused-ring structure rather than fatty acid chains.
questions.explain: A steroid is recognized by its four fused rings sharing edges, three six-membered and one five-membered. Oestradiol and testosterone both have this structure, which is non-polar and lets them pass through the phospholipid bilayer.

questions.q: A polypeptide of 150 amino acids is assembled by condensation reactions. How does the number of water molecules change as the whole chain is formed?
options: 150 released
300 released
149 released
149 consumed
optionWhy: A student who counts one water molecule per amino acid picks this. In fact one water molecule is released per peptide bond, and 150 amino acids are joined by 149 peptide bonds, because the two ends of the chain are unreacted.

A student who counts both the amine and the carboxyl group of every amino acid as releasing water picks this. In fact one peptide bond uses one carboxyl group and one amine group together and releases a single water molecule, so the total is 149.

Each condensation reaction links two amino acids with one peptide bond and releases one molecule of water. Joining 150 amino acids into one chain needs 149 peptide bonds, so 149 water molecules are released.

A student who thinks water is a reactant in condensation picks this. In fact water is a product: it is formed from the –OH of a carboxyl group and the –H of an amine group and released, so 149 molecules are produced, not used up.
questions.explain: Each condensation reaction links two amino acids with one peptide bond and releases one molecule of water. Joining 150 amino acids into one chain needs 149 peptide bonds, so 149 water molecules are released.

questions.q: An enzyme's activity at its optimum pH of 7 was 100 units. One sample was placed at pH 2 for 10 minutes, then returned to pH 7: its activity was 4 units after 1 hour and 4 units after 24 hours, and its polypeptide chains were found to be intact. A second sample was cooled to 5 °C for 10 minutes, then returned to 37 °C: its activity was 100 units. What do these results show?
options: The low pH denatured the enzyme, changing its conformation in a way that was not reversed at pH 7, whereas the low temperature did not denature it.
Both treatments denatured the enzyme, but the denaturation caused by cooling was reversed when the sample was warmed again.
The acid-treated enzyme was only temporarily denatured and would have regained full activity if left for longer at pH 7.
The acid hydrolysed the peptide bonds of the enzyme, so its polypeptide chains were broken into separate amino acids.
optionWhy: The pH 2 sample lost almost all activity and did not recover even after 24 hours at the optimum pH, while its chains stayed intact: its shape had changed permanently, which is denaturation. The cooled sample regained full activity, so its conformation was unchanged.

A student who thinks both sides of the temperature graph are explained by denaturation picks this. In fact low temperature does not change a protein's shape; it only slows molecular movement, so full recovery on warming shows the enzyme was not denatured.

A student who expects a protein to refold once conditions are restored picks this. In fact the activity was the same after 1 hour and after 24 hours, showing no recovery; denaturation is in most cases permanent.

A student who thinks denaturation breaks peptide bonds picks this. In fact the chains were found to be intact, so the loss of activity was due to a change of shape, not to breakdown of the primary structure.
questions.explain: The pH 2 sample lost almost all activity and did not recover even after 24 hours at the optimum pH, while its chains stayed intact: its shape had changed permanently, which is denaturation. The cooled sample regained full activity, so its conformation was unchanged.

questions.q: A lipid is found to form a continuous sheet-like bilayer when shaken with water. Which property must the lipid have?
options: It must be entirely hydrophobic, so that all of its molecules cluster together away from water.
It must be amphipathic, with a hydrophilic region and a hydrophobic region in each molecule.
It must be able to form covalent bonds with neighbouring lipid molecules in the sheet.
It must be acted on by an enzyme that assembles the molecules into the bilayer.
optionWhy: A student who thinks lipids are simply water-repelling picks this. In fact an entirely hydrophobic lipid would separate as a droplet; a sheet needs a hydrophilic part that stays in contact with water.
Only amphipathic lipids form bilayers: the hydrophilic regions face the water on each side and the hydrophobic regions form the core. Phospholipids are the main example in cell membranes.
A student who expects the sheet to be a covalent polymer picks this. In fact a bilayer is held together only by hydrophobic interactions and other weak forces.
A student who thinks bilayers must be built picks this. In fact the bilayer forms spontaneously; the test in the stem involves only lipid and water, with no enzyme.
questions.explain: Only amphipathic lipids form bilayers: the hydrophilic regions face the water on each side and the hydrophobic regions form the core. Phospholipids are the main example in cell membranes.

questions.q: An animal cell with a cytoplasmic solute concentration of 0.30 mol dm⁻³ is placed in a solution with a solute concentration of 0.10 mol dm⁻³. The membrane is impermeable to the solute. What happens?
options: Water leaves the cell by osmosis, because water moves from the higher to the lower solute concentration.
Net water movement is into the cell, because more free water molecules hit the membrane from the outside.
Solute diffuses out of the cell until both sides reach 0.20 mol dm⁻³, and water then follows the solute out.
No water crosses the membrane, because the cell membrane has no aquaporins to let water pass.
optionWhy: A student who applies 'high to low' to the solute picks this. In fact net water movement is from the lower solute concentration (0.10) to the higher (0.30), so water enters the cell.

The solution outside has the lower solute concentration and so a higher proportion of free water molecules. Water molecules move randomly in both directions, but more cross inwards than outwards, so the net movement is into the cell.
A student who treats osmosis as solute diffusion picks this. In fact the stem says the membrane is impermeable to the solute, so the solute cannot move; it is water that crosses.
A student who thinks aquaporins are the only route for water picks this. In fact water can cross the bilayer slowly without them, so osmosis still occurs; aquaporins only increase its rate.
questions.explain: The solution outside has the lower solute concentration and so a higher proportion of free water molecules. Water molecules move randomly in both directions, but more cross inwards than outwards, so the net movement is into the cell.

questions.q: Membrane proteins from a mouse cell and from a human cell were labelled with different coloured markers and the two cells were fused. After about 40 minutes the two colours were fully intermixed over the surface of the fused cell. What does this show?
options: Proteins can move laterally through the bilayer, so the membrane is fluid and proteins are not held in a fixed pattern.
The membrane developed gaps as it became more fluid, allowing the labelled proteins to leak through them.
The proteins from the two cells were covalently bonded into a single new continuous sheet during fusion.
The proteins remained in fixed positions but the mosaic pattern was rearranged by the fusion event.
optionWhy: If the proteins had been fixed in place, each colour would have stayed on its own half. Their mixing shows that proteins move sideways through the fluid phospholipid bilayer, which is what 'fluid' means in the fluid mosaic model.
A student who thinks 'fluid' means leaky picks this. In fact the bilayer stays continuous; proteins mixed by moving sideways within the plane of the membrane, not through gaps in it.
A student who expects membrane components to be covalently linked picks this. In fact no bonds form between the proteins; they mix because the bilayer is fluid and they can diffuse through it.
A student who thinks 'mosaic' means a fixed arrangement picks this. In fact the proteins moved: fusion joins the membranes but does not move a protein from one half to the other.
questions.explain: If the proteins had been fixed in place, each colour would have stayed on its own half. Their mixing shows that proteins move sideways through the fluid phospholipid bilayer, which is what 'fluid' means in the fluid mosaic model.

questions.q: Liver cells were broken open in a cold, isotonic, buffered solution and the homogenate was spun in an ultracentrifuge at a series of increasing speeds. Only the pellet formed at the second speed consumed oxygen and produced ATP when supplied with substrates. What does this investigation illustrate about how progress in science is made?
options: Electron micrographs of the organelles in the second pellet would have revealed the same function, so the centrifuge added little that was new.
A technique for isolating one type of organelle made it possible to test its function directly, which could not be done before.
The ATP must have come from intact cells surviving in the pellet, since organelles cannot work once removed from a cell.
A single spin at the highest speed would have brought every organelle down in one pellet that could be tested just as well.
optionWhy: A student who thinks organelle functions were read off from images picks this. A micrograph shows structure only; oxygen consumption and ATP production could only be demonstrated by isolating the organelle and testing it, which needed the ultracentrifuge.

Differential centrifugation separated a fraction rich in mitochondria, and that fraction alone respired. Study of the function of individual organelles became possible once ultracentrifuges and cell fractionation methods had been developed: progress in science often follows a new technique.

A student who extends cell theory to mean that nothing smaller than a cell can carry out a process picks this. Isolated mitochondria in a suitable solution consume oxygen and make ATP; that is exactly what makes cell fractionation informative.

A student who thinks centrifuging merely speeds up settling picks this. A single high-speed spin would bring down every organelle together; only a series of increasing speeds separates nuclei, then mitochondria, then smaller components into different pellets. A mixed pellet could not show which organelle was responsible for the oxygen consumption.
questions.explain: Differential centrifugation separated a fraction rich in mitochondria, and that fraction alone respired. Study of the function of individual organelles became possible once ultracentrifuges and cell fractionation methods had been developed: progress in science often follows a new technique.

questions.q: A phagocyte engulfs a bacterium into a phagocytic vacuole, and lysosomes then fuse with the vacuole. What is the advantage of digesting the bacterium inside this compartment rather than in the cytoplasm?
options: The enzymes could safely be released anywhere in the cell, so the vacuole serves only to hold the bacterium still.
Hydrolytic enzymes reach a high concentration around the bacterium while being unable to digest the phagocyte's own contents.
The vacuole makes its own enzymes on its membrane, so the lysosomes only add more membrane to enlarge it.
Digestion in the cytoplasm would be too rapid to control, so the vacuole membrane slows the enzymes' access to the bacterium inside.
optionWhy: A student who believes enzyme specificity makes lysosomal enzymes harmless picks this. Released into the cytoplasm they would hydrolyse the phagocyte's own proteins and membranes; the vacuole keeps that process separate.

Fusion delivers the lysosomal enzymes into the small volume of the vacuole, so they act on the bacterium at high concentration, and the vacuole membrane separates this incompatible process from the rest of the cytoplasm. Both advantages of compartmentalization apply.

A student who thinks vacuoles produce digestive enzymes picks this. A phagocytic vacuole has no enzymes of its own; it is the fusion of lysosomes that supplies them, which is the whole point of the fusion.
A student who thinks membranes exist to slow processes down picks this. The compartment speeds digestion by concentrating enzyme and substrate together; it does not throttle it.
questions.explain: Fusion delivers the lysosomal enzymes into the small volume of the vacuole, so they act on the bacterium at high concentration, and the vacuole membrane separates this incompatible process from the rest of the cytoplasm. Both advantages of compartmentalization apply.

questions.q: In an early-stage embryo a signalling protein is made by cells at one end and spreads towards the other end. Cells at three different distances from the source develop into three different cell types. Which explanation is best supported?
options: The protein is an on/off switch, so the cells that received it differ from the cells that did not.
Different genes are switched on above different concentrations, so each position expresses its own set.
Each cell's fate was fixed internally at fertilization; the protein only marks the region afterwards.
The protein removes different genes from cells at different distances, so each type keeps only the genes it needs.
optionWhy: A student who treats a signal as present or absent picks this. An on/off switch could divide the embryo into two cell types only; three types at three distances show that cells respond to the level of the protein, not merely to its presence.

The protein forms a concentration gradient. Cells respond to the concentration they experience, with different genes switched on at different thresholds, so cells at high, medium and low concentration express different genes and differentiate into three types.

A student who thinks fate is programmed inside each cell from the start picks this. The cells are genetically identical and unspecialized; the gradient is what makes their gene expression differ, so the protein is a cause, not a label.
A student who thinks differentiation removes genes picks this. All the cells keep the whole genome; the gradient changes which genes are expressed at each position, not which genes are present.
questions.explain: The protein forms a concentration gradient. Cells respond to the concentration they experience, with different genes switched on at different thresholds, so cells at high, medium and low concentration express different genes and differentiate into three types.

questions.q: A cell taken from a 4-cell human embryo can develop into a complete individual with its own placenta. A cell from the inner cell mass of a blastocyst can form any tissue of the body but not a placenta. A stem cell from adult bone marrow forms only blood cells. How should the three cells be classified?
options: Totipotent for both embryo cells, then multipotent.
Totipotent, then pluripotent, then finally multipotent.
Totipotent, then pluripotent for both of the others.
Pluripotent for both embryo cells, then finally multipotent.
optionWhy: A student who thinks all embryonic cells stay totipotent picks this. The inner cell mass cell cannot form the placenta, so it has already become pluripotent; totipotency is lost within the first few divisions.
Forming a whole individual including the placenta is totipotency. Forming any body tissue but not the placenta is pluripotency. Forming only the cell types of one tissue, here blood, is multipotency.
A student who believes adult stem cells can form any cell type picks this. The bone marrow cell forms only blood cells, which is the limited range that defines a multipotent stem cell.
A student who uses pluripotent and totipotent interchangeably picks this. A cell that can form the placenta as well as the embryo is totipotent; pluripotent cells cannot form extra-embryonic tissue.
questions.explain: Forming a whole individual including the placenta is totipotency. Forming any body tissue but not the placenta is pluripotency. Forming only the cell types of one tissue, here blood, is multipotency.

questions.q: Which statement about the range of cell size in humans is correct?
options: Red and white blood cells and gametes are all about 10 µm across.
The egg and the sperm are similar in size, as each supplies half the DNA.
A motor neuron can be over a metre long, yet only micrometres wide.
A muscle fibre several centimetres long must be a chain of short cells.
optionWhy: A student who assumes all cells are one generic size picks this. Red blood cells are 7–8 µm, white blood cells mostly about 10–20 µm, a sperm head about 5 µm and an egg about 100 µm across.

A student who carries the equal genetic contribution over to cell size picks this. The egg, about 100 µm across, is one of the largest human cells; the sperm is one of the smallest, because it carries almost no cytoplasm.

Cell size is an aspect of specialization. A single motor neuron running from the spinal cord to a muscle in the foot has an axon over a metre long, while its width remains microscopic; extreme length suits its function of carrying signals over a distance.

A student who thinks no single cell can be visible picks this. A striated muscle fibre is a single continuous unit with one plasma membrane that can run for centimetres; its length is part of its specialization.
questions.explain: Cell size is an aspect of specialization. A single motor neuron running from the spinal cord to a muscle in the foot has an axon over a metre long, while its width remains microscopic; extreme length suits its function of carrying signals over a distance.

questions.q: A student argues: 'Real cells are not cubes, so the cube model of surface area-to-volume ratio proves nothing about real cells.' Which response best evaluates this claim?
options: The claim is right: a model is only valid when it has the same shape as the thing that it represents.
The model is simplified on purpose; area and volume scale in the same way for any shape, so its conclusion holds.
The claim is right for another reason: in real cells the surface area and the volume grow in proportion.
The claim is wrong, because in real cells the ratio increases with size, which the simple cube model fails to show.
optionWhy: A student who judges a model by its resemblance to the real thing picks this. The value of a model lies in the relationship it isolates, not in looking like the system; the cube model isolates the effect of size and does so correctly.

Models are simplified versions of complex systems. Cubes are simpler than real cells, but scaling a shape of any kind multiplies area by the square and volume by the cube of the scale factor, so the conclusion that larger cells have a smaller ratio applies to real cells.

A student who scales area and volume in step picks this. In any object, cube or cell, area grows with the square of length and volume with the cube, so they do not grow in proportion; the cube model shows exactly this.

A student who believes the ratio rises with size picks this. In real cells, as in cubes, the ratio falls as size increases; the cube model shows this correctly, which is why the claim is wrong for a different reason.
questions.explain: Models are simplified versions of complex systems. Cubes are simpler than real cells, but scaling a shape of any kind multiplies area by the square and volume by the cube of the scale factor, so the conclusion that larger cells have a smaller ratio applies to real cells.
